**Finding: deviation (Section 7.5(b), paragraph p0346)** — validated redline submitted.

**What I found.** The Agreement contains no licence grant in our favour anywhere. The only provision touching the topic is the transition covenant in Article VII, which expressly disclaims any licensing obligation:

> "The Servicer will not be obligated to provide, license or assign its processes, procedures, models, servicing software or other applications to any Successor Servicer or any third party..."

I checked Article III (servicing), Article IX and the definitions for any grant of Cellco systems, software or marks (searches for "license", "intellectual property", "servicing software", "trademark") — nothing else exists.

**Why it fails.** The rule's walk-away trigger is a licence where affiliates and contractors are excluded with no path to add them. Here the position is worse than revocable-at-will: the Servicer has an absolute right to refuse, so on a servicing transfer neither the Issuer, its Affiliates, nor the Successor Servicer (the contractor who would actually run the platform) has any right to the servicing systems. That defeats both the preferred and the fallback position, and it operates against us as Issuer/Depositor — so the direction test is satisfied.

**The edit.** Minimal surgery on the same sentence: it now grants a non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to the Issuer, its Affiliates and its contractors (including any Successor Servicer), transferable to successors, scoped only to what is necessary to service the Receivables. I deliberately preserved the Servicer's legitimate carve-outs for genuine third-party transfer/confidentiality restrictions and for legal, regulatory, privacy and data protection limits — narrowing them to *unaffiliated* third parties so the exception cannot swallow the grant.

Confidence 0.72: the substantive gap is clear, though this is an ABS transfer and servicing agreement rather than a licence-driven deal, and a resisting Servicer may push back on platform licensing for genuine proprietary-systems reasons.
